name: Pathology Detection and Scan Triage
title: Pathology Detection and Scan Triage
answer: Pathology detection and scan triage systems examine medical images such as X-rays, CT scans, MRIs, and pathology slides to flag suspicious findings and order cases by urgency. The scope includes detecting fractures, bleeds, tumors, and other abnormalities, and separating normal studies from those needing immediate human review. These tools sit within diagnostic imaging and radiology as decision support, not replacement for a radiologist or pathologist. They are used in emergency departments, screening programs, and routine reporting queues.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Pathology detection and scan triage systems examine medical images such as X-rays, CT scans, MRIs, and pathology slides to flag suspicious findings and order cases by urgency. The scope includes detecting fractures, bleeds, tumors, and other abnormalities, and separating normal studies from those needing immediate human review. These tools sit within diagnostic imaging and radiology as decision support, not replacement for a radiologist or pathologist. They are used in emergency departments, screening programs, and routine reporting queues.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These models typically run on hospital picture archiving and communication systems, radiology information systems, or cloud-based inference services. They require access to DICOM images and often use GPU servers for near real-time processing. Some deployments run on edge devices inside imaging machines for immediate triage. Integration depends on HL7 and FHIR messaging to move results into the electronic health record.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by training convolutional neural networks or vision transformers on large labeled datasets of medical images. Radiologists or pathologists annotate the images to teach the model which pixels or regions indicate disease. At inference, the model produces a heatmap, bounding box, or risk score that a human reviews. Triage models often use a threshold on that risk score to reorder worklists, while detection models highlight areas for closer inspection.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on patient safety, data provenance, and liability. Training data must come from consented or de-identified sources, and the model's performance must be validated on local patient populations before use. If a triage tool misses a critical finding or delays a diagnosis, questions of product liability and clinical accountability arise. Active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies illustrate the legal exposure in this area. Provenance records should document the training data, model version, and any human overrides for each case.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: These systems are moving toward multimodal models that combine imaging with lab results and clinical notes for more accurate triage. Regulatory pathways are tightening around continuous monitoring and real-world performance reporting. Future work will likely focus on reducing false negatives in rare diseases and on explainable outputs that radiologists can trust. The field is also shifting from single-disease detectors to generalist models that can flag many conditions in one pass.
